chunks: From him, from Abu Ja'far, from Abu al-Jawza', from al-Husayn ibn 'Ulwān, from 'Amrū ibn Khālid, from Zayd ibn 'Alī, from his fathers (peace be upon them), who said:

The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'When two Muslims meet each other with their swords, the killer and the killed are in the Fire.' It was said: 'O Messenger of Allah, [why is the] killer [in the Fire]?' He said: 'Because he intended to kill.' Then [implied: the killed is also in the Fire because he also intended to kill, though the text explicitly quotes the reason for the killer, the context implies the same for the killed as per the first clause].

key_terms.عَلَى غَيْرِ سُنَّةٍ: Not for a specific reason (such as war or justice)

ai.seo_question: Why are both the killer and the killed in Hellfire when two Muslims fight?
ai.summary: This hadith, recorded in Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, highlights the Shia jurisprudential principle that mutual intent for combat (*qatl*) leads to shared punishment, distinguishing it from cases where one party fights defensively. While the killer is punished for his active aggression, the slain is held accountable for his sincere intention to kill, illustrating that mere survival does not absolve one of spiritual liability in a duel of equals. This nuance is central to understanding the ethics of conflict in Shia tradition, where internal disposition (*niyyah*) carries significant weight alongside external action.
